Ancient Siberian tomb reveals surprising secrets of cannabis use 2,800 years ago

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (956 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A remarkable discovery in a nearly 2,800-year-old Siberian tomb has provided the oldest directly dated archaeological evidence that people used cannabis for its intoxicating effects.
  • Cannabis is among the most widely used psychoactive plants in the modern world, but tracing its use thousands of years into the past presents a major archaeological challenge.
  • Gino Caspari, affiliated with the Institute of Archaeological Sciences at the University of Bern and the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology, investigated an elaborate tomb in the Republic of Tyva in southern Siberia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A remarkable discovery in a nearly 2,800-year-old Siberian tomb has provided the oldest directly dated archaeological evidence that people used cannabis for its intoxicating effects. By examining ancient cannabis seeds and chemical traces preserved in human hair, researchers have uncovered new clues about the role of the plant in prehistoric burial rituals.

Cannabis is among the most widely used psychoactive plants in the modern world, but tracing its use thousands of years into the past presents a major archaeological challenge. Flowers, leaves, and resins tend to decompose over time, leaving little physical evidence behind. Ancient communities also relied on cannabis for practical purposes, including producing fiber and oil, making it difficult to distinguish these uses from medicinal or recreational consumption.

An international team led by Dr. Gino Caspari, affiliated with the Institute of Archaeological Sciences at the University of Bern and the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology, investigated an elaborate tomb in the Republic of Tyva in southern Siberia. The burial site belonged to prominent members of the Scythians, a culture known for its skilled horseback riders who inhabited the vast Eurasian steppe.

Ancient Siberian Tomb Contains 1,000 Cannabis Seeds.

Industry observers note that during the investigation, researchers recovered approximately 1,000 cannabis seeds from the tomb. They used radiocarbon dating to determine the age of six individual seeds. Combined with other dating evidence, the results indicate that the seeds were deposited in the burial site during the early eighth century B.C.

"The seeds show that cannabis played an key role in the rituals surrounding the burial," claims Caspari, an archaeologist and the study's lead author.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers also analyzed human hair preserved in the tomb's central burial chamber. Chemical evidence in several samples pointed to cannabis consumption, providing a crucial connection between the plant remains and the people buried at the site.

"This study is particularly insightful because it combines the analysis of plant remains with molecular traces in the human body," claims Caspari.

The findings were published in the journal Science.

Chemical Traces in Ancient Hair Reveal Cannabis Use.

According to recent reports, although the cannabis seeds were remarkably well preserved, their presence alone could not establish whether the plant was used for its mind-altering effects. The seeds probably came from wild cannabis plants, and researchers could not determine whether people had deliberately cultivated them for their psychoactive properties.

The strongest evidence came from the preserved human hair. Using high-resolution mass spectrometry and other analytical techniques, the team identified clear chemical signals consistent with cannabinol (CBN) in several samples.

Sources indicate that CBN can form when tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the primary compound responsible for cannabis intoxication, undergoes oxidation. The researchers also detected weaker signals that matched the mass of THC, further supporting the possibility that the individuals had consumed cannabis.

It has been revealed that while these chemical findings indicate cannabis use, they cannot reveal how much was consumed or exactly how the compounds entered the body. The individuals may have inhaled cannabis smoke or consumed the plant in another way, but the available evidence cannot establish a particular method.

Other archaeological discoveries from later periods in Central Asia provide clearer evidence of cannabis inhalation. At those sites, researchers have identified cannabinoid residues on heated stones and inside vessels, pointing to the use of heat to release compounds that could be inhaled.

"The molecular traces in the hair and the cannabis seeds come from the same grave and suggest that cannabis was used for its intoxicating properties," claims Caspari, who conducts research at the Institute of Archaeological Sciences at the University of Bern and the Max Planck Institute for Geoanthropology in Jena (Germany).

Cannabis, Horse Sacrifices, and Ancient Burial Rituals.

The cannabis evidence was discovered within an elaborate ceremonial burial site, suggesting that the plant may have been connected to important Scythian funerary traditions.

"In this princely tomb, the burials were accompanied by extensive horse sacrifices and, most likely, human sacrifices as well," says Gino Caspari.

Earlier research at the site identified the remains of 18 horses that had been deliberately positioned on the burial mound. Continued excavations have since uncovered evidence of several dozen more sacrificed horses, along with scattered human bones.

These discoveries reveal the extraordinary scale of the burial ceremonies and provide important context for understanding why cannabis may have been included among the materials deposited in the tomb.

Oldest Directly Dated Evidence of Cannabis Intoxication.

Taken together, the seeds and chemical traces in human hair represent the oldest directly dated archaeological evidence right now known for cannabis use associated with intoxication.

However, several questions remain unanswered. The researchers cannot determine how much THC the ancient cannabis contained, whether the plants were particularly potent, or whether Scythian communities had begun deliberately selecting or cultivating cannabis varieties with higher concentrations of psychoactive compounds.

To investigate these questions, the team is now studying genetic material recovered from the ancient plant remains. The unusually good preservation of the cannabis DNA could provide valuable insights into how humans domesticated the plant and how it spread across different regions over thousands of years.

Industry observers note that "We have already begun sequencing some of the plant samples," says Gino Caspari. "DNA preservation is excellent in this case. This will help us learn more about the history of the domestication and spread of this crop soon.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon told CNBC on Monday that financing demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure remains strong despite recent market jitters as investors reassess the risks involving the massive build-out.

Solomon said that his firm has been "very active" in AI capital markets deals over recent weeks, a setup that he expects to continue.

"There's still very strong demand for investments in the AI infrastructure build and the technology around the growth of AI," Solomon told CNBC's Leslie Picker.

Changes in the political environment are among factors that will "create recalibrations and ups and downs, and we're seeing some of that," Solomon mentioned. "But I still deeply believe in the long-term trajectory of the power of AI in our economy to drive productivity.".

AI-related stocks, including chipmakers and neocloud providers, have tumbled in recent weeks as investors reassess whether the hundreds of billions of dollars being poured into AI infrastructure will generate good returns.

Recent findings suggest that the selloff, which began before the U.S. midterm elections, intensified after Democrats scored sweeping victories on Tuesday, raising concerns that political opposition could slow the industry's expansion.

In a recent development, the shifting sentiment comes at a key moment for AI model lab Anthropic, which is preparing for a potential IPO that could become one of the biggest tests yet of public-market appetite for AI companies. Goldman is among the banks leading that IPO process.

"We'll see, obviously, if this IPO moves forward, how it all plays out," Solomon stated, declining to comment in detail about the IPO. "I would say that the market environment is still pretty constructive.".

Solomon also pushed back against political resistance to data center construction, arguing that the infrastructure is essential to the U.S. economy and that it can be built responsibly.

"We certainly don't want this infrastructure going to places outside the U.S., which is what will naturally happen because the demand for compute is there," Solomon said.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The Last Animal: Human History and the Fate of Life on Earth from the Ice Age to the Sixth Extinction Kyle Harper Princeton Univ.
  • In The Last Animal, historian Kyle Harper asks a provocative question: how have humans affected animal biodiversity?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that human activities such as hunting and agriculture have put pressure on populations of Sumatran orangutans, which are now critically endangered. Credit: Getty.

The Last Animal: Human History and the Fate of Life on Earth from the Ice Age to the Sixth Extinction Kyle Harper Princeton Univ. Press (2026).

In The Last Animal, historian Kyle Harper asks a provocative question: how have humans affected animal biodiversity?

In a recent development, explorations of species loss driven by humans are nothing new. But other books tend to focus either on the present day or on prehistory — the extinction of ice-age animals such as woolly mammoths and dire wolves, for instance. The Last Animal offers a continuous account of biodiversity from prehistoric times to the present day.

What does the future hold for the thawing Arctic?

What does the future hold for the thawing Arctic?

Assembling a historical account on this scale is a Herculean task. But, Harper argues, it is only by zooming out that people can appreciate how slow changes in humanity’s relationship with other species have led to the current biodiversity crisis. Humans have been reshaping animal communities for millennia, long before written records of extinction existed. By reflecting on how humanity got here, he contends, we give ourselves the best chance of turning things around.

According to recent reports, the book is a triumphant piece of scholarship, both rigorous and engaging. And Harper’s ability to draw on ecology, Earth science and environmental history is impressive. At the same time, the book reveals limitations in previous research approaches. And it highlights how a lack of crosstalk between research fields prevents scholars from seeing the full picture.

Harper begins by discussing the spread of ancient humans across the world, starting with the emergence of Homo erectus nearly two million years ago. Human dispersal coincides with a marked disappearance of large animals from the fossil record. The reasons for this are uncertain. Some scientists point to climate change, but Harper suspects human hunting activity. There is strong evidence that humans were involved in the extinction of many turtle species, for example, which must have been easy and delicious prey for hungry hunters.

Humans were shaping animal life long before the dawn of farming, Harper notes. Mutually beneficial relationships with cattle, llamas and dogs, for instance, opened the door to domestication and selective breeding. And in Cyprus, prehistoric settlers intentionally introduced wild boar and fallow deer as game, permanently changing the island’s ecosystem.

Motorized vessels and industrial fishing practices have reshaped marine ecosystems.Credit: Getty.

Later, deforestation and urbanization affected biodiversity. Since medieval times, commercial fishing has disrupted intricate marine food webs. And from the nineteenth century onwards, industrial farming, railways, refrigeration and pharmaceutical drugs have made it possible to raise vast numbers of cattle and battery hens in unnaturally good health, and in locations far from the cities that they eventually feed. These transformations in how humans live have had unintended and often surprising side effects on animal species. In the 1990s in India, for example, farmers gave the painkiller diclofenac to their ageing cattle, not realizing that it would remain in their systems and poison any vultures that fed on their carcasses. The birds experienced a sharp population decline as a result.

Recent findings suggest that writing about history with such a wide scope requires evidence from many disciplines. Harper’s chapters on prehistory lean heavily on fossils, archaeological finds and ancient DNA. Meanwhile, his historical chapters draw mainly on written records, including colonial accounts of animal extinctions that occurred as a result of European imperial expansion.

AI tools can design genomes. Will they upend how life evolves?

Industry observers note that AI tools can design genomes. Will they upend how life evolves?

According to recent reports, in part, this split reflects the fact that there are limited ways to learn about events that pre-date the invention of writing. But, Harper stresses, academic fields have also maintained somewhat arbitrary limitations on the time periods that they cover. For example, during the nineteenth century, when it became apparent that humans had existed for many millennia, historians decided to study only events that occurred after the advent of writing. They ceded “the murky time before written texts” to archaeologists, anthropologists and Earth scientists.

Recent findings suggest that yet, many changes in biodiversity span that boundary. Although the last woolly mammoths (Mammuthus primigenius) died out at the same time as Egyptian pharaohs ruled, their disappearance was part of a process that began during the Ice Age.

Even when extinctions are well documented, their causes and ecological consequences can remain difficult to disentangle. For instance, European arrival in, and later settlement of, the Mascarene Islands in the Indian Ocean during the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries led to the loss of more than 50 animal species, including the dodo (Raphus cucullatus). Researchers don’t know to what extent introduced plants, animals and diseases contributed to these extinctions, or how colonial deforestation and hunting might have affected the island’s animals. These extinctions could be studied using a variety of scientific tools, from ecological modelling to ancient-genome analysis — but these opportunities have remained under-explored.

A few woolly mammoths survived on Wrangel Island in the Arctic until about 4,000 years ago.Credit: David Zorrakino/Europa Press/Getty.

The former prosecutor, Guillermo Zuany Portillo, shepherded C.I.A. officers for more than six months beginning last year as they trained forces in his state, Chihuahua, joined those forces on counter-cartel missions and provided expertise during ground operations, a New York Times investigation revealed this week.

In a recent development, ms. Sheinbaum expressed fury at the C.I.A.’s presence during raids in Chihuahua and denied knowledge of the agency’s activities. On Wednesday, she said in a regular morning news conference that investigations into matter must continue.

“It’s worth finding out who this person is and how he worked with one of the U.S. agencies,” she said of Mr. Zuany.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Louis Carr has exited his post as president of BET less than a year after he was elevated to the role.

In a recent development, in a note sent to staff on Monday (Nov. 16), Skydance co-chair/chief content officer George Cheeks shared that Carr “has decided to leave the tech giant after an extraordinary career at BET,” where he worked for four decades.

Cheeks wrote that Carr “has been one of BET’s greatest champions, helping shape the brand, its business and its connection to Black audiences and culture. Louis built lasting partnerships with some of the world’s leading brands and helped cement BET as a cultural force. As President, he led BET with clarity and purpose, creating renewed momentum for the brand. His passion, vision and heart have been front and center in everything he does, and it has been a privilege to partner with him.”.

Cheeks added that Carr will remain at BET through the end of the year and that more will be shared about the firm’s “leadership and structure” at a later date.

Last December, it was confirmed that Carr would succeed Scott Mills, who served as BET president/CEO for 23 years. Carr was previously president of media sales. His appointment followed Paramount Global’s $8 billion merger with Skydance Media in August 2025. Paramount had been shopping BET since 2023, before announcing it was no longer for sale ahead of the Skydance merger.

In a recent development, just last month, Carr spoke with Billboard about the revamped Soul Train Awards, which is set to air on Nov. 27 following a two-year hiatus. The show was taped Nov. 5 in Chicago.

In a recent development, “It’s an iconic brand,” Carr told Billboard at the time, citing R&B’s current popularity as a factor in the reboot. “When we paused it two years ago, consumers in the community spoke and very loudly, asking, ‘Why would we do that?’ So I always knew it was one of the main things on my agenda to bring back because it’s crucial to our culture, our community and our industry. And I wanted to bring it back to its hometown Chicago, the best place to revitalize [the brand].”.

According to recent reports, “We find ourselves in a space where there aren’t a lot of people celebrating Black people, Black history and Black entertainment,” Carr added. “And that’s our job.”.

#679. A nuclear blast could save Earth from an asteroid, but there's a catch

📅 08 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1253 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

A nuclear blast could save Earth from an asteroid, but there's a catch

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1253 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A nuclear explosion could potentially protect Earth from an incoming asteroid by releasing powerful X-rays that heat its surface and push it onto a safer trajectory.
  • Unlike the smooth, round objects often used in computer simulations, real asteroids have uneven surfaces and irregular shapes.
  • Recent findings suggest that A newly introduced study published in Icarus found that changing the direction of an X-ray burst could produce vastly different results, even when targeting the same asteroid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A nuclear explosion could potentially protect Earth from an incoming asteroid by releasing powerful X-rays that heat its surface and push it onto a safer trajectory. However, new research suggests that the success of such a mission could depend heavily on which side of the asteroid receives the blast.

Unlike the smooth, round objects often used in computer simulations, real asteroids have uneven surfaces and irregular shapes. Those differences can dramatically influence how an asteroid moves when exposed to intense radiation.

Recent findings suggest that A newly introduced study published in Icarus found that changing the direction of an X-ray burst could produce vastly different results, even when targeting the same asteroid. In one simulation, the asteroid's speed changed by 3.9 millimeters per second when irradiated from one direction, compared with only 0.8 millimeters per second from another. That represents a nearly fivefold difference in deflection velocity, the change in the asteroid's forward speed caused by the burst.

"We expected aim to matter," said Nathan Moore, a physicist at Sandia National Laboratories who led the research. "What surprised us was how much.".

The effects on an asteroid's rotation could be even more dramatic. For another simulated asteroid, the change in how rapidly it spun varied by a factor of 17 depending on the direction of the X-rays.

These findings suggest that understanding an asteroid's shape and carefully selecting where to direct a nuclear blast could be essential to protecting Earth from a future impact.

The research received funding through Sandia's Laboratory Directed Research and Development program.

A Newly introduced Way to Simulate Asteroid Deflection.

To investigate how different asteroid shapes respond to nuclear blasts, Moore and his colleagues developed what they describe as the most accurate asteroid deflection model yet.

Earlier computer models faced a major limitation. Researchers typically had to choose between representing an asteroid's complex shape and performing highly detailed calculations of the physical forces involved. Combining both approaches demanded more computing power than was practical.

The new system overcomes that obstacle, allowing scientists to study realistic asteroid shapes while maintaining the precision needed to calculate their response to an X-ray burst. The result is the most detailed simulation of asteroid deflection produced so far.

Industry observers note that "Our upcoming algorithm is over 1,600 times faster, which was critical to this breakthrough," Moore said. "With the old models, computers just couldn't handle it.".

Why Lumpy Asteroids Change Everything.

According to recent reports, moore's interest in improving these calculations grew out of an earlier experiment using Sandia's Z machine. That experiment provided the first demonstration that X-rays could deflect a small piece of asteroid material.

The next challenge was determining how the same physical process might affect an entire asteroid.

"I started wondering how to scale up the calculation to more accurately predict deflection of a full-scale asteroid.".

According to recent reports, A major problem was the widespread practice of treating asteroids as spheres. Although this simplifies the mathematics, it overlooks the irregular shapes of real asteroids, which can have ridges, depressions, and uneven surfaces.

"You can make estimates that way, but asteroids come in all kinds of odd, lumpy shapes," he mentioned. "That's when I latched onto some work one of my colleagues was doing related to outgassing of objects in space. I think we had an aha moment when we realized we could do this. No more spheres. We would be able to model deflection for any asteroid.".

The solution involved bringing together two sophisticated simulation systems already used at Sandia for very different types of physical problems.

"The ALEGRA code is normally used to model fast, high-energy experiments, like magnetically imploding wires on the Z machine, while SPARTA, a direct simulation Monte Carlo code, is usually used to model comparatively weak, slowly evolving forces, like the drag on a satellite from the solar wind," Moore explained.

"The key innovation here was figuring out how to combine the two simulation approaches.".

Predicting What Happens After a Nuclear Blast.

Industry observers note that the newly introduced computer model allows researchers to reconstruct an asteroid using detailed 3D images captured during spacecraft flybys. They can then simulate a nuclear X-ray burst while adjusting the explosion's strength, its distance from the asteroid, and the direction from which the radiation arrives.

The software calculates how much material would vaporize across different parts of the asteroid's surface and displays the results as a heat map. Using that information, it estimates the resulting push, changes in the asteroid's rotation, and the extent of surface damage.

In a recent development, these calculations are important because a successful planetary defense mission would ideally change an asteroid's trajectory without breaking it into multiple dangerous fragments. Redirecting one large object could be preferable to creating several pieces that might still threaten Earth.

However, the simulations cannot yet predict every possible consequence of a nuclear blast.

Industry observers note that "Right now, our computer model only considers breakup of rocks on the surface. We can't predict breakup of the entire asteroid body accurately yet," Moore noted.

It has been revealed that developing that capability will require additional research, investment, and more advanced computational tools. An intense X-ray burst can trigger numerous physical effects, some of which influence one another. Accounting for all those interactions makes it exceptionally difficult to predict exactly how an asteroid would behave during a real deflection attempt.

Choosing the Right Blast Could Save Earth.

Despite these remaining challenges, the findings offer valuable guidance for future planetary defense efforts. The research demonstrates that the direction of a nuclear blast is not simply a minor detail. It can substantially change how effectively an asteroid is redirected.

According to recent reports, "Our study shows how important it is to aim carefully," Moore remarked. "Pick the right side and you win. Guess wrong and it could be a bad day.".

According to recent reports, the new simulation tools could eventually help mission planners identify the most effective way to deflect a threatening asteroid. In principle, researchers could enter detailed information about its shape, then calculate the ideal explosive strength, distance, and direction needed to move it away from Earth.

Turning those calculations into a real mission would still be extremely difficult.

Industry observers note that for one thing, the software requires reasonably accurate information about the asteroid's shape from every direction. If an asteroid were discovered on a collision course with Earth, there might not be enough time to gather the necessary observations.

Sources indicate that another challenge would be delivering and positioning a nuclear device at precisely the right location relative to an asteroid traveling through space. Even if scientists could identify the ideal blast configuration, executing it would require extraordinary precision.

In a recent development, nevertheless, the improved simulations could eliminate much of the uncertainty surrounding one possible method of asteroid defense. By better understanding how nuclear X-rays interact with the complex surfaces of real asteroids, scientists are moving closer to predicting which strategies would work best.

For Moore, that progress is an encouraging step toward ensuring humanity has a better chance of preventing a catastrophic asteroid impact.

Materials provided by Sandia National Laboratories. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

LSU star Angel Reese defended the gesture she aimed at Iowa Hawkeyes’ Caitlin Clark near the end of the Tigers’ first NCAA women’s basketball national championship victory on Sunday, saying “I don’t take disrespect lightly.”.

Reese could be seen approaching Clark before moving her open hand in front of her face – popularized by WWE star John Cena to mean “you can’t see me” – before pointing to her ring finger in a gesture some interpreted as a reference to the place her newly-acquired championship ring might sit.

Caitlin Clark breaks records galore during historic March Madness run.

Clark made a similar gesture to another player earlier in the tournament.

The gesture has sparked much debate, especially on social media. Some have criticized Reese, while others have defended her actions, highlighting how there was no public outrage in response to Clark’s gesture earlier in the tournament.

Sports journalist Jose de Jesus Ortiz called Reese’s actions “classless,” while former ESPN host Keith Olbermann called Reese an “idiot” for the gesture.

In the press conference after the victory, Reese referenced the difference in reaction she received as a result of her gesture as compared to the one Clark received.

In a recent development, “All year, I was critiqued for who I was. I don’t fit the narrative,” Reese noted. “I don’t fit the box that y’all want me to be in. I’m too hood. I’m too ghetto. Y’all told me that all year. But when other people do it, and y’all don’t say nothing.

In a recent development, “So this is for the girls that look like me. For those that want to speak up for what they believe in. It’s unapologetically you. And that’s what I did it for tonight. It was bigger than me tonight. And Twitter is going to go into a rage every time.

Recent findings suggest that “And I’m happy. I feel like I’ve helped grow women’s basketball this year. (…) I’m looking forward to celebrating and then next season.”.

LSU beats Iowa to win its first NCAA women's basketball championship.

Reese had 15 points and 10 rebounds in the 102-85 victory and won the women’s March Madness’ Most Outstanding Player award.

In the post-game broadcast, Reese referenced the similar gesture Clark made to a Louisville opponent in the Elite Eight.

Sources indicate that in the same game, Clark stated to an opponent: “You’re down by 15 points. Shut up,” according to the Bleacher Report.

Recent findings suggest that “Caitlin Clark is a hell of a player but I don’t take disrespect lightly,” Reese said. “She disrespected [LSU’s] Alexis [Morris] (…) and I wanted to pick her pocket. But I had a moment at the end of her game. I was in my bag, I was in my moment.”.

After the Championship game, Clark herself said she didn’t notice anything at the time.

“I was just trying to get to the handshake line and shake hands and be grateful that my team was in that position,” Clark remarked in the post-game press conference. “All the credit in the world to LSU. They were tremendous. They deserve it. They had a tremendous season.

According to recent reports, “(LSU head coach) Kim Mulkey coached them so, so well. She’s one of the best basketball coaches of all time, and it indicates. She only said really kind things to me in the handshake line, so I’m very grateful of that too.

It has been revealed that “But honestly I have no idea. I was just trying to spend the last few moments on the court with especially the five people that I’ve started 93 games with and relishing every second of that.”.

LSU head coach Mulkey mentioned she had “no clue” about what transpired.

Among those defending Reese on social media were ESPN’s Holly Rowe and former NBA star Etan Thomas.

Sources indicate that “People hating on Angel Reese or Caitlin Clark. Stop. Unapologetically confident young women should be celebrated NOT hated. Get used to it,” Rowe wrote on Twitter.

According to recent reports, former Washington Wizards, Oklahoma City Thunder and Atlanta Hawks player Thomas wrote: “Hold on now!!!! It was cute when Caitlin Clark did it. Y’all didn’t have any challenges with it at all. So don’t be all outraged and talking about class and sportsmanship when Angel Reese does the same thing. We’re not doing double standards here.”.

Reese noted the negative reaction on social media throughout the season has helped fuel her excellent season, having finished averaging 23.0 points and 15.4 rebounds in her first season with LSU after transferring from Maryland.

“Twitter can say what they want to say,” she said. “I love reading those comments. I have all the screenshots of what everybody has said about me all season. What are you going to say now?”.

#675. Latest Update: I saw Saturn’s rings in seconds with the Celestron StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian telescope — full review

Latest Update: I saw Saturn’s rings in seconds with the Celestron StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian telescope — full review

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1955 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian is a great model to learn the basics of manual telescope operation and get great views of your chosen targets, thanks to intuitive smartphone integration, but it isn't as easy to set up as you might think.
  • Why you can trust Space.com Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you.
  • Sources indicate that saturn was only a night past its annual opposition when I pointed the Celestron StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian straight at it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian is a great model to learn the basics of manual telescope operation and get great views of your chosen targets, thanks to intuitive smartphone integration, but it isn't as easy to set up as you might think.

Sharp, high-contrast 150mm optics.

Difficult and heavy to lift and move.

Why you can trust Space.com Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test and review products.

Sources indicate that saturn was only a night past its annual opposition when I pointed the Celestron StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian straight at it. The planet was at its biggest and brightest of the year, the seeing was good and its famous rings were visibly opening up after appearing edge-on from Earth in recent years. It was an obvious target for a latest telescope.

Finding it took seconds. After selecting Saturn in Celestron’s StarSense Explorer app, I followed the on-screen arrows as I moved the telescope across the sky. As I got closer, the app zoomed in until a bullseye turned green. I looked through the supplied 25mm eyepiece, then swapped to the 10mm to see a pale yellow Saturn at 75x magnification, with its rings sharply defined and its giant moon Titan visible in orbit.

In a recent development, it was a stunning view, and exactly the kind of experience a beginner needs from a first telescope. There was no frustration and no wondering whether I was looking in the right place. StarSense took me straight there — but, crucially, I moved the telescope myself. I’ve always liked that combination of hand-holding and DIY observing that Celestron’s StarSense tech gives you.

According to recent reports, I’m less convinced by the tabletop telescope it’s attached to. Although this $599 RRP (£379) model is significantly smaller than the Celestron StarSense Explorer 8-inch Dobsonian telescope I’ve previously reviewed, it still weighs 25 lbs (11.33 kg). You need to place it on something sturdy before you can use it comfortably. After living with it in my backyard, I’m not convinced the tabletop format is the advantage it initially appears to be.

In a recent development, I’ve used Celestron’s StarSense Explorer system on a variety of telescopes and have always been impressed by how easy this type of smartphone navigation is to use. The technology works just as well here and, for me, it remains one of the best ways of making a traditional optical telescope accessible to a complete beginner.

Recent findings suggest that this isn’t a computerized GoTo telescope. There are no motors to slew across the sky automatically and no tracking system to keep an object centered. Instead, a smartphone sits in a dock attached to the telescope, and its camera looks at the sky via a small mirror. Celestron’s StarSense Explorer app analyzes the reflections of the stars it sees, works out exactly where the telescope is pointing and tells you which direction to push it to reach the object you want to observe.

My iPhone 16 Pro Max fitted perfectly into the dock, and the initial alignment process was identical to what I’d used before. Once that was done, I used StarSense to find the Pleiades (M45), the Andromeda Galaxy (M31), the Double Cluster in Perseus and Saturn. It worked every time, with the target appearing in the eyepiece when the app told me I had reached it.

Sources indicate that I can find all of those objects without an app, but that’s not really the point. Beginners often struggle to translate a star chart or an astronomy app into actual telescope movements. StarSense gives you confidence that you’re heading in the right direction while still requiring you to operate it physically.

Recent findings suggest that that makes it a useful way to learn the night sky. After repeatedly pushing the telescope from one familiar object to another, you begin to understand how everything fits together. That’s very different from pressing a button and watching a GoTo or smart telescope move itself, and it’s why I think StarSense is worth paying extra for, even on a relatively wide-field telescope like this one.

The StarSense system may be the headline feature, but the reason to buy any Dobsonian is aperture. This one uses a 150mm (5.9-inch) parabolic primary mirror with a 750mm focal length and a relatively fast f/5 focal ratio. That combination gives it fairly low-power, wide-field views that are particularly well suited to large star clusters.

In a recent development, the Pleiades was one of my favorite views. At 30x through the supplied 25mm eyepiece, the telescope gave me a sharp field of stars and a particularly good view of what I call “Carter’s Whip” — the curving line of stars running through the cluster. I saw little obvious softness towards the edges, and focusing was straightforward.

The Andromeda Galaxy (M31) was a different proposition. From my light-polluted backyard, I could see Andromeda’s bright core, but not its outskirts or its satellite galaxies. That’s largely a consequence of observing a galaxy from a city, not a criticism of a 150mm telescope, but it’s a useful reminder of what visual astronomy is actually like. Don’t expect the colorful, detailed views of galaxies and nebulas you see in astrophotos, such as the stacked images a smart telescope can give you.

Saturn was more rewarding, but I would have liked more magnification when the seeing was this good. Add a Barlow lens if planets are a priority — it can double the magnification of any eyepiece you use it with.

Overall, I was impressed by the telescope’s optics. The views were sharp and contrast-y, and there’s enough aperture here to make a serious start in visual astronomy. However, the two supplied 25mm and 10mm Kellner eyepieces are decidedly entry-level — and obvious candidates for upgrading in the medium term.

In a recent development, the focuser is a weak point. It’s a fairly basic 1.25-inch rack-and-pinion design, but I noticed some wobble and vibration while using it. That’s a shame because the focuser is one of the parts of a telescope you constantly interact with, and something smoother and more precise would make the entire instrument feel more accomplished.

The tabletop design isn’t necessarily as convenient as it sounds. I expected this scope to feel considerably more convenient than Celestron’s 8-inch StarSense Dobsonian. The base has built-in grab handles, but the assembled telescope's shape and weight make it awkward to lift onto a table — I certainly wouldn’t recommend it to anyone with a bad back. You could move the optical tube and base separately, but that starts to cancel out the convenience of owning a relatively compact tabletop telescope.

You also need to choose your table carefully. It has to be sturdy enough not to introduce vibrations, but not so large that you have to stretch across it to reach the eyepiece as the telescope points to different parts of the sky. I found myself bending and stretching into some awkward positions.

Once it’s in position, the Dobsonian mount worked well. The balance was good, and I didn't need to adjust the altitude tension, while the movements offered a useful mix of resistance and fluidity as I followed StarSense around the sky. At 75x, however, keeping Saturn centered was more difficult than I expected. It was easy to over-nudge the telescope, then correct in the opposite direction.

Celestron sells an optional tripod for the telescope, and after using the tabletop base, I can see why that might be attractive. However, I’d personally rather put the money towards a larger Dobsonian whose base is designed to sit directly on the ground.

This scope doesn’t arrive in one piece. Assembly took about 90 minutes, and it required all manner of screws and screwdrivers. The main problem was getting the screws into the holes in the Dobsonian base, which took so much effort that I ended up with a blister on my hand. That’s not what I expected from a telescope aimed at beginners, especially when almost everything about using it has been designed to make things easy.

Once built, things improved considerably. My review sample arrived well collimated, so I didn’t have to adjust the mirror alignment. The tube rings, phone dock and general construction were all good enough for a telescope at this price, and nothing about the telescope felt particularly fragile. Once the telescope is outside, on a suitable table and aligned, it’s an impressively straightforward instrument to use.

Sources indicate that the more I used the StarSense Explorer 150mm Dobsonian, the more I wondered who really benefits from the tabletop format. It’s certainly smaller than Celestron’s 8-inch StarSense Explorer Dobsonian, but it’s still a substantial object to store, and I didn’t feel any more inclined to grab it for a quick observing session.

In a recent development, going bigger offers an optical advantage. An 8-inch/203mm aperture collects about 83% more light than a 150mm aperture, which matters when you’re observing faint deep-sky objects. The 8-inch StarSense also had a much nicer 2-inch Crayford focuser, and generally felt like a telescope with a little more room to grow into.

In a recent development, dobsonians are the perfect companion to smart telescopes. The latter have completely changed what beginners can photograph from their backyards, particularly under light pollution. They can reveal galaxies and nebulas that are extremely difficult or impossible to see visually. I use them all the time. But they are no substitute for navigating to and actually seeing objects in the night sky with your own eyes.

The two approaches don’t need to compete. A smart telescope has to be pointed and then left alone for an hour or four to stack images. That time could be spent pushing something like the StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian around the sky, and actually looking through an eyepiece at the same objects. One highlights you far more than your eyes can detect, but the other lets you see the photons yourself — and make a human connection with the night sky.

Sources indicate that at $599 RRP (£379), the StarSense Explorer 150mm sits in an interesting part of the beginner telescope market. There are smaller tabletop Dobsonians like the Celestron Moon Mission 100mm without smartphone navigation, but I think StarSense is worth paying extra for, particularly for a first-time telescope owner.

In a recent development, if you mainly want to observe planets and the moon, a refractor like the Celestron StarSense Explorer LT 70AZ also makes sense. However, if you want to go relatively large, I do recommend the StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian — with an key qualification. Its optics are good, StarSense is superb, and it’s an excellent way for a beginner to learn their way around the night sky, but I’m not convinced that 150mm is the sweet spot for this particular design. It’s too significant to feel genuinely convenient as a tabletop telescope, yet not big enough to deliver the full advantages of a larger Dobsonian.

If space is tight, this is a very capable first telescope. If you have room for the 8-inch StarSense Explorer, I’d go bigger.

Jamie is an experienced science and travel journalist, stargazer and eclipse chaser who writes about exploring the night sky, solar and lunar eclipses, the Northern Lights, moon-gazing, astro-travel, astronomy and space exploration. He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.

Boeing said Monday that it looks to cut 5% of its commercial airplane workforce as its production ramp-up is moving at a slower pace than the organization expected.

The cuts will be through a combination of attrition and layoffs, Stephanie Pope, head of the commercial aircraft unit, said in a memo to staff.

Pope reiterated that the company is still working to stabilize production rates of its bestselling 737 Max planes, which are made outside of Seattle.

CEO Kelly Ortberg told investors last month that the firm won't significantly increase production of the Max aircraft until the second half of next year. He said the company's wing production has been slower than expected.

"Unfortunately, that means we need to align our staffing levels to our revised business blueprint, resulting in a reduction of approximately 5% through a combination of attrition and involuntary layoffs, with notifications beginning in December.".

Boeing is targeting a production rate of 52 planes a month in the second half of 2027. Ortberg stated the tech giant has been trying to stabilize output at a rate of about 47 of its 737 Max planes a month.

An ancient ocean full of giant predators reveals a surprising twist in evolution

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (745 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, an extraordinary collection of fossils in central Colombia is revealing a surprising chapter in Earth's evolutionary history.
  • Scientists from McGill University and the Centro de Investigaciones Paleontológicas (CIP) identified this unusual pattern while studying fossils from Colombia's Paja Formation.
  • Drawing on these findings, McGill biology professor Hans Larsson and PhD graduate Dirley Cortés have proposed a latest concept called a "Biotic Inflection." The term describes an evolutionary turning point when older groups nearing extinction coexist with newer lineages that are beginning to expand and diversify.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, an extraordinary collection of fossils in central Colombia is revealing a surprising chapter in Earth's evolutionary history. Researchers have uncovered evidence of a time when ancient animal groups that were approaching extinction lived alongside newer groups that would eventually flourish. The discovery suggests that major evolutionary transitions can occur without the widespread destruction associated with mass extinctions.

Scientists from McGill University and the Centro de Investigaciones Paleontológicas (CIP) identified this unusual pattern while studying fossils from Colombia's Paja Formation. The ancient marine ecosystem preserves an exceptional mixture of surviving Jurassic lineages and emerging Cretaceous groups, offering a rare glimpse into a period of profound biological change.

Drawing on these findings, McGill biology professor Hans Larsson and PhD graduate Dirley Cortés have proposed a latest concept called a "Biotic Inflection." The term describes an evolutionary turning point when older groups nearing extinction coexist with newer lineages that are beginning to expand and diversify.

A Perfect Storm for Ancient Ocean Biodiversity.

Industry observers note that the researchers believe an unusual combination of environmental conditions helped make this remarkable coexistence possible. Warm greenhouse temperatures, elevated sea levels, and coastal waters rich in nutrients may have supported an unusually diverse range of marine life.

In a recent development, another notable factor was the emergence of new ocean connections between the eastern Pacific and the early Atlantic through the region that is now Colombia. Together, these conditions likely created opportunities for different groups of animals to thrive within the same ecosystem. Many of these environmental influences continue to shape biodiversity around the world today.

In a recent development, "The Paja Formation records an extraordinary process in the history of life, when a 'perfect storm' of environmental factors we know to promote ecological complexity coincided with ancient lineages that were about to disappear. At the same time, new groups were beginning to flourish," Larsson noted.

A Lost World of Giant Marine Reptiles and Predators.

Recent findings suggest that the evidence comes from the Early Cretaceous Paja Formation near Villa de Leyva, Colombia. This fossil-rich region has preserved an astonishing variety of prehistoric marine animals, providing scientists with an unusually detailed picture of an ancient ocean ecosystem. Most of the fossils collected from the formation are housed at the CIP.

In a recent development, "This geological formation has produced an exceptionally rich fossil record that includes giant marine reptiles like long-necked plesiosaurs and marine crocodile relatives, as well as turtles, sharks, crustaceans and others," Cortés explained. "Together, these animals formed the Paja Biota, one of the most ecologically complex marine communities found to date.".

In a previous study, the researchers reconstructed the feeding relationships among animals in the Paja Biota. Their analysis revealed an exceptionally intricate food web, with an unusually large variety of apex predators occupying the highest levels of the ecosystem.

This remarkable complexity makes the Paja Formation especially valuable for investigating how ecosystems change as older evolutionary groups decline and new ones become established.

Could This Discovery Change How Scientists Understand Evolution?

Industry observers note that the proposed Biotic Inflection offers a potentially important fresh way to understand major changes in Earth's biodiversity. Rather than being driven by a mass extinction, some evolutionary transitions may involve periods of extraordinary diversity, when declining lineages and emerging groups coexist.

Sources indicate that however, the researchers emphasize that more evidence is needed to establish how common this pattern may have been. Additional fossil discoveries, more accurate estimates of fossil ages, and comparisons with geological formations in other parts of the world will help determine whether similar transitions occurred elsewhere in Earth's history.

"I think we've discovered a latest model of global biodiversity change. Now we'll need to see just how widespread this could be in Earth's history and how we can quantify its impacts," Larsson said.

The research received funding from the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada, the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute, the Anders Foundation, the 1923 Fund, Gregory D. and Jennifer Walston Johnson, the Fonds de recherche Nature et technologies Québec, and the McGill Biology Department Writing-Year Award 2024-2025.

#667. A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster

📅 07 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1532 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1532 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles.
  • Sources indicate that but position and time are different.
  • According to recent reports, the discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles. Werner Heisenberg's famous uncertainty principle states that certain properties, such as a particle's position and momentum, cannot both be measured with unlimited precision. This restriction is not caused by flaws in scientific instruments. It is built into the laws of nature.

Sources indicate that but position and time are different. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle does not impose the same restriction on these quantities. Now, researchers have experimentally demonstrated another fundamental limitation: an electron's location and its behavior over time cannot both be determined with arbitrary precision. Known as the "space-time limit," this newly observed relationship could have major implications for the future of quantum technology and ultrafast electronics.

According to recent reports, the discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs. Jascha Repp, Rupert Huber, Franz Giessibl, and Klaus Richter, along with a team at the Max Planck Institute in Hamburg led by Angel Rubio.

Watching Electrons Move at Incredible Speeds.

Sources indicate that understanding how matter behaves at the smallest scales is essential for developing the next generation of technology. Advances in clean energy, quantum computing, and powerful electronics for artificial intelligence all depend on knowing how chemical reactions unfold, how light interacts with materials, and how electrons travel through electronic devices.

In a recent development, however, even the sharpest microscopic photographs cannot reveal the full picture. Scientists also need to observe how these processes change over time, effectively creating slow-motion movies of events occurring at the atomic scale.

In a recent development, at RUN, researchers are developing ultrafast microscopes capable of recording the movements of electrons, atoms, and molecules with extraordinary precision in both space and time. About ten years ago, scientists in Regensburg used ultrafast scanning tunneling microscopy to resolve the movement of a single molecule across space and time for the first time.

In a recent development, tracking individual electrons presents an even greater challenge. At these microscopic distances, electrons can move roughly a thousand times faster than atoms and molecules, with notable changes taking place over just attoseconds.

It has been revealed that to appreciate how extreme these scales are, consider that an atom is approximately ten million times smaller than a millimeter. An attosecond is one-billionth of a billionth of a second. The difference between an attosecond and a second is comparable to the difference between one second and the entire age of the universe.

It has been revealed that making these measurements is especially difficult because electrons do not behave like ordinary objects. Their motion follows the unusual laws of quantum mechanics rather than the familiar rules of classical physics.

Ultrafast Lasers Reveal Quantum Tunneling.

Industry observers note that to observe electron behavior at these extraordinary speeds, the researchers built a fresh laser system that provides much finer time resolution than earlier experiments. The system allows them to control and study the quantum motion of individual electrons directly.

According to recent reports, in the experiments, carefully timed laser pulses drive electrons from an extremely sharp metal tip toward a silver surface. The distance they travel is only a few atomic diameters.

The researchers detect this movement by measuring the resulting electrical current. To determine exactly when the electrons move, they use two pulses of light separated by a precisely controlled interval.

Simon Maier, the lead author of the paper, explains: "By varying the time interval between the two laser pulses, we can directly observe how the electrons respond.".

Industry observers note that this approach revealed clear evidence of electron motion occurring on attosecond timescales. It revealed that the laser pulses could transfer electrons within these incredibly brief intervals while allowing scientists to observe the process as it happened.

What makes the result particularly remarkable is how the electrons travel. Instead of moving like conventional particles, they behave as quantum waves. This allows them to pass through an energy barrier separating the metal tip from the silver surface, even though classical physics predicts they should not have enough energy to cross it.

This phenomenon, known as quantum tunneling, is somewhat like an object passing through a solid wall without breaking or damaging it.

"Our measurement can be understood as a high-speed camera for the electron wave packets, since you can see at what point in time the tunneling process takes place," explains Katharina Glöckl, a doctoral student and co-author of the publication.

A Surprising 500-Attosecond Delay.

In a recent development, to understand the measurements more deeply, researchers working with Prof. Angel Rubio performed sophisticated quantum simulations of the electrons' behavior near the "space-time limit.".

Their calculations closely reproduced the experimental findings and uncovered another remarkable detail. The electrons did not respond to the light field instantaneously. Instead, their motion lagged behind it by approximately 500 attoseconds.

At such extreme scales, several fundamental features of quantum physics become vital simultaneously.

Sources indicate that for example, the researchers found that the laser pulses could not be described entirely by treating light as a wave or entirely by treating it as individual particles called photons. Their effects displayed characteristics of both descriptions. This combination was essential for exploring electron behavior so close to the "space-time limit.".

The team also discovered that controlling electron motion over extremely short intervals changes how the electrons are distributed in space. Quantum mechanics describes these electrons using wave packets, which represent how their wave properties extend across different locations.

The relationship between the timing of electron motion and the spatial extent of these wave packets revealed the central limitation behind the discovery.

A Hidden Tradeoff Between Space and Time.

Raffael Spachtholz, another co-author of the study, explains: "The more precisely we want to pin down the electron's position in time, the more energy we need to provide. And as a result, the electron wave packet spreads out more spatially.".

In other words, improving the precision of an electron's timing comes with a cost. The more tightly researchers define when its motion occurs, the more broadly its quantum wave packet spreads through space.

To examine this relationship experimentally, the team placed a single atom on the surface to confine the electron wave packets to an extremely small region immediately before the laser pulses arrived.

This setup allowed the scientists to directly measure the connection between the electrons' spatial distribution and the timing of their motion.

Importantly, even when the electrons received substantial energy from the laser pulses, their wave packets remained sufficiently localized for microscopy with atomic spatial resolution and attosecond time resolution.

The findings provide experimental insight into a fundamental space-time constraint that scientists had previously only suspected. They also make it possible to systematically investigate how changes in electron motion over time affect the spatial structure of quantum wave functions.

Could Quantum Electronics Become Hundreds of Thousands of Times Faster?

Beyond revealing a upcoming aspect of quantum behavior, the discovery could open the door to technologies that operate on timescales far beyond the capabilities of today's electronics.

One especially promising possibility involves using precisely controlled electron wave packets to influence chemical reactions.

Transferring a single electron to a molecule represents the smallest possible transfer of electric charge. But when that electron is concentrated within an exceptionally small region of space and time, the resulting local peak current density can reach as much as 1 trillion amperes per square centimeter.

Such extreme conditions could give scientists upcoming ways to control chemical bonds and observe how molecules change during reactions.

Recent findings suggest that "In the future, we want to use such wave packets to specifically trigger chemical reactions and observe, on the relevant length and time scales, how chemical bonds can be broken or altered," explains Prof. Jascha Repp enthusiastically.

The implications could extend well beyond chemistry. Greater control over electron motion may eventually help engineers develop electronic devices and quantum information systems that operate at speeds approaching the fundamental limits of electron dynamics.

According to recent reports, "In the long term, the insights gained could also contribute to operating electronics and quantum information processing at the intrinsic speed limit of electron motion itself -- hundreds of thousands of times faster than the at the moment dominant CMOS technology," adds Prof. Rupert Huber.

That possibility remains a long term technological goal rather than an achievement demonstrated in the current experiments. Nevertheless, the findings provide a upcoming foundation for exploring how electrons can be manipulated at the smallest distances and shortest timescales.

For Repp and Huber, the results suggest that the range of potential applications is extraordinarily broad. They believe that future advances in controlling electrons at the space-time limit may ultimately depend more on human creativity than on the constraints imposed by nature.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that paul Barril’s offer to African dictators was straightforward: Your opponents will be subjected to surveillance and manipulation.
  • Plenty of heads of state took up the services he offered, including Omar Bongo in Gabon and Denis Sassou-Nguesso in Congo.
  • Barril was often described in the news media as a former French “supergendarme” for his longtime work in elite units.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that paul Barril’s offer to African dictators was straightforward: Your opponents will be subjected to surveillance and manipulation. Newspapers will be “infiltrated.” Plots against the state will be “neutralized.”.

Plenty of heads of state took up the services he offered, including Omar Bongo in Gabon and Denis Sassou-Nguesso in Congo. Other clients went to Paris to do their shopping at his Security Action Store, which offered the latest in bulletproof vests or night-vision goggles, as Mr. Barril recounted in one of his six autobiographies, “The Elysee’s Secret Wars” (1996).

Mr. Barril was often described in the news media as a former French “supergendarme” for his longtime work in elite units. After he left the gendarmerie, or national police, in 1984, he became a security adviser and mercenary provider across the African continent and was implicated by human rights groups in the Rwandan genocide of 1994.

His death, on Oct. 20 at 80 at his home in Antibes, France, was announced by the French interior ministry. He had Parkinson’s disease.

By the time he founded his mercenary-security firm, Secrets, a French acronym for Security Equipment Planning and Realization Company, in 1984, Mr. Barril was a well-chronicled public figure.

In the gendarmerie, which in France is under the military, he joined a fresh military police intervention unit, the GIGN, in 1974. The French news media chronicled Mr. Barril’s reputation as an ultrafit top cop, a military-grade swimmer and diver, a black belt in karate, a parachutist, a hostage liberator and a policeman working inside and outside the law. With the GIGN, he participated in the 1979 operation against Islamist militants who had seized the Grand Mosque in Mecca, taking dozens hostage.
